title: C++ foundations
blurb: The language as far as your notes go: initialisation, types and sizes, scope, linkage, namespaces and enums. No loops, no classes — none of these need them.
goal: Finish this and every idea in chapters 0 to 2 of your notes has been tested rather than only read.

title: Writing C++, a step at a time
blurb: Twelve programs in prerequisite order: a condition, then a loop, then a function, then a container. Each one needs only what the one before it introduced.
goal: Finish this and you can read input, decide, repeat, split work into functions, and hold data in a vector, a string and a map - which is most of what small C++ programs are made of.

title: Building what the library gives you
blurb: The standard library's simplest tools, written out: a search, a count, a binary search, a stack, a ring buffer and a growable array. Available in C++ and Python.
goal: Finish this and std::find, std::lower_bound, std::stack and std::vector stop being magic - you will know what each one costs and why its interface is shaped the way it is.

title: Simulating the machine
blurb: Six small programs that each stand in for a piece of real hardware or a real kernel: byte order, cache lookup, page replacement, CPU scheduling, a state machine and a shift register.
goal: Finish this and the diagrams in a computer architecture or operating systems chapter become things you have already built, so the numbers in them mean something.

title: Rust foundations
blurb: Ownership, borrowing, slices, Option, Result and the ? operator - in that order, because each one is the answer to a question the previous one raises.
goal: Finish this and you will know what the borrow checker is actually checking, and why a Rust function signature tells you more than a C++ one does.

title: First steps
blurb: Ten problems across the whole site, chosen so that each one needs only what the one before it taught. A reasonable first week.
goal: A tour of what is here, without hitting anything that needs background you have not got yet.

title: How memory really behaves
blurb: Alignment, cache lines, locality, virtual memory and the page-fault path — the thread that runs from sizeof all the way to a 4.5x slowdown from a loop order.
goal: Be able to explain why two loops doing identical arithmetic differ by eight times.

title: What the standard does not promise
blurb: Signed overflow, integer promotions, out-of-bounds reads, and the optimiser deleting a check you wrote. The most useful thing a C++ programmer can be frightened of.
goal: Stop reading "it worked at -O0" as evidence of anything.

title: Problems you write code for
blurb: Every code problem on the site, easiest first. Each compiles and runs for real, in C++ if you want it to.
goal: Six working programs, each one a thing worth having written once.

title: Metric spaces, from the axioms up
blurb: Distance as four conditions rather than a formula, and then everything that follows from them: balls, open and closed sets, convergence, completeness, continuity and a first look at compactness.
goal: Finish this and the definitions stop being things you look up and start being things you reason with — including the ones where the answer depends on which space you are standing in.

title: Probability, in the order it makes sense
blurb: Sample spaces and counting first, because most errors are made before any arithmetic; then conditioning, independence, random variables, expectation and variance, and a first continuous distribution.
goal: Finish this and the two mistakes that cause most of the damage — reversing a conditional, and treating disjoint as independent — are ones you can see coming.

title: Writing hardware, and watching it run
blurb: Five designs you write in SystemVerilog and simulate in this tab — a 2-to-1 multiplexer and a 4-to-1, a counter, an edge detector and a state machine that finds a pattern — with the waveform beside each one. The questions around them are the vocabulary: what blocking assignment does to a shift register, what the fabric actually contains, and where the clock rate comes from.
goal: Finish this and a timing diagram is something you can read off a trace rather than something you take on trust. It is simulation throughout: nothing here says a design would synthesise, meet timing, or work on a device, and the exercises say so.

title: Project: a ring-buffer event logger
blurb: One program over three files and three milestones: a bounded queue, a policy for what to do when it is full, and a view over what it holds. Your files are carried forward from each milestone to the next, and each one re-runs everything the ones before it asked for.
goal: Finish this and you have written a ring buffer you would actually use, across separately compiled translation units, with every earlier requirement still passing.

title: Project: a synchronous FIFO
blurb: Two modules in two files: a parameterised block of storage with a registered read, and the pointers and flags that turn it into a queue. The second milestone instantiates the first, so the two really do have to work together.
goal: Finish this and you have written the structure every hardware design eventually needs, with the full/empty boundary and the one-cycle read latency pinned down rather than hoped for.

title: Metric Spaces, the whole unit
blurb: The seven chapters of the Metric Spaces unit as one tree: definitions and examples, limits and uniform convergence, completeness and Banach, open and closed sets, connectedness, sequential compactness, compactness. Every node says which section and page of the notes it comes from.
goal: Finish this and every chapter of the unit has been tested rather than only read, with the non-examinable material marked as such so you know what you are allowed to skip.

title: Probability 2, the whole unit
blurb: The seven chapters of Probability 2 as one tree: foundations and the strong law, random walks and Wald, Markov chains, Poisson processes, continuous-time chains and queues, martingales, Brownian motion. Every node says which section and page of the notes it comes from.
goal: Finish this and each chapter has been exercised on its own terms - a difference equation for the walks, a matrix for the chains, a martingale for the stopping theorems - rather than as one undifferentiated subject.

title: Project: a cache simulator
blurb: One program over three files in three directories, and three milestones: taking an address apart, choosing what to throw out, and deciding when memory finds out. Your files are carried forward from each milestone to the next, and each one re-runs everything the ones before it asked for.
goal: Finish this and the cache diagrams in an architecture chapter are things you have built - the index, the ways, the dirty bit and the writeback - rather than things you have read about.

title: Project: a sequence detector
blurb: Four SystemVerilog modules built up over three milestones: a detector whose pattern is an input, a saturating counter, a top that is nothing but wiring, and an arming gate. The same counter is instantiated twice at the end, which is the point of having made it a module.
goal: Finish this and you have composed a small design out of separately written modules, with the interface between them doing the work that a specification is supposed to do.

title: Programs that are already wrong
blurb: Seven complete programs, each with one defect in it, across C++, Rust, Python and SystemVerilog. Every one of them is correct on the obvious inputs and wrong on the ones nobody wrote a test for, which is why they are worth meeting on purpose.
goal: Finish this and you have met the common shapes once each: an iterator invalidated, a last group never flushed, an off-by-one in a modulus, a register that is a cycle late, and a combinational block that is secretly a latch.
